questions.q: What does defense in depth mean for a public API?
questions.explain: No single check stops everything. Rate limits, CORS, CSRF, authentication, validation and safe headers each stop different attacks, and together one mistake is not a breach.
options: One very strong check at the start of every request
Several independent checks in a row, so an attack that gets past one layer is stopped by the next
Hiding the API address so attackers cannot find it
Checking every request twice with the same function

questions.q: How does ZudoJS split security work between @zudojs/security and @zudojs/http?
questions.explain: The security package answers questions like "is this origin allowed?" and knows nothing about servers. The http package wraps those answers into middleware you put in front of your routes.
options: @zudojs/security has plain building-block functions; @zudojs/http has middleware built on them
@zudojs/security is the web server; @zudojs/http only has status codes
They do the same thing, so you pick one of them
@zudojs/http is for browsers and @zudojs/security is for servers

questions.q: Your API runs behind one load balancer that you operate. What should you pass to extractClientIp?
questions.explain: Behind your proxy, every request seems to come from the proxy. trustProxy: 1 reads the address your proxy added and ignores whatever the client wrote before it. Trusting the whole header would let clients fake their address again.
options: trustProxy: 1, the number of proxies you run
trustProxy: true, to trust every address in the header
Nothing: always use remoteAddress, even behind a proxy

questions.q: The in-memory limiter allows max: 5 login attempts. You run three copies of the Task API. How many attempts can an attacker make per window?
questions.explain: The counts live in one process's memory, so each copy allows 5. It still slows guessing a lot, but for an exact limit across servers you need a shared store such as Redis.
options: 5, because the limit is in the code
1, because the copies divide the limit
Up to 15, because each process counts on its own
Unlimited, because in-memory limiters do not work with several copies

questions.q: In the attack test, https://evil.example fetched /tasks and got status 200 but allow-origin = null. What protects the user?
questions.explain: CORS is enforced by the browser, not the server, so the status is still 200. The missing Access-Control-Allow-Origin header is what makes the browser refuse to show the response to the script.
options: The status 200 means the attack failed
The server deleted the response body
Without Access-Control-Allow-Origin, the browser hides the response from the evil page's script
Nothing: the evil page can read the tasks

questions.q: Why does @zudojs/security refuse { origin: "*", credentials: true }?
questions.explain: credentials: true lets the browser send cookies. With "*", any site could send them and read the answer. List the exact origins instead.
options: Because "*" is not a valid string
It would let every website on the internet act as your logged-in user
Because credentials only work over plain HTTP
Because an array is faster than "*"

questions.q: You want to allow only https://app.example.com with a RegExp. Which one is safe?
questions.explain: Anchor both ends with ^ and $. Without them, https://app.example.com.evil.example or https://evil-app.example.com can match. An array of exact strings is even safer.

questions.q: The Task API sends its JWT in an Authorization header that your own JavaScript adds. When do you need CSRF tokens?
questions.explain: Another website cannot make the browser add your Authorization header. Cookies are attached automatically, so the moment the token moves into a cookie, add CSRF protection. CORS only hides responses; the forged request still arrives.
options: Only once credentials are sent automatically by the browser, which means cookies
Never, because CORS already stops forged requests

questions.q: Why was the attacker's POST with Mallory's own valid CSRF token refused for Ada's session?
questions.explain: A token signed for session-mallory does not match session-ada. That is why you always pass sessionId both when you issue and when you verify.
options: Each token is tied to one session by sessionId, at issue time and at verify time
Tokens can only be used once per day

questions.q: CSRF protection lets safe methods like GET through without a token. What rule follows from that?
questions.explain: A GET passes without a token, so a GET that deletes or updates something would be open to forged requests. Changes belong in POST, PUT, PATCH or DELETE.
options: Put the CSRF token in the URL of every GET
Use GET for deletes, since it is simpler
Never change data in a GET handler
Turn CSRF protection off for the whole API

questions.q: What does the HttpOnly cookie attribute do?
questions.explain: HttpOnly hides the cookie from JavaScript, so an injected script cannot steal it. Secure means HTTPS only, and SameSite controls sending it on requests from other sites.
options: Sends the cookie only over HTTPS
Stops page scripts from reading the cookie
Stops the cookie from being sent by other sites
Deletes the cookie when the tab closes

questions.q: What does the CSP rule script-src 'self' protect against?
questions.explain: It allows only scripts from your own origin. An injected inline script is blocked. That makes CSP the strongest browser-side defence against XSS; 'unsafe-inline' weakens it.
options: XSS: a script an attacker injected into the page will not run
Requests from other origins to your API

questions.q: When should you send Strict-Transport-Security (HSTS)?
questions.explain: HSTS tells the browser to use only HTTPS for a long time. Sent too early, it can lock users out of HTTP-only parts. preload asks browsers to hard-code your domain as HTTPS-only, which is hard to undo.
options: Right away, even while parts of the domain only work over HTTP
Once your whole domain works over HTTPS, and think carefully before keeping preload

questions.q: A user pastes http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/ into your "link preview" feature. Why is that dangerous?
questions.explain: Your server sits inside your network, so it can reach addresses the attacker cannot. Making your server send requests for an attacker is Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF).
options: It is a very large page that is slow to fetch
It is the cloud metadata service: your server can reach it and it hands out the server's cloud credentials
It contains JavaScript that runs in the user's browser
It is not dangerous, because it is not a domain name

questions.q: isSafeUrl("https://preview.attacker.example/page") returns true. What must you still do before fetching it?
questions.explain: isSafeUrl cannot see DNS. An attacker can point a normal-looking name at 169.254.169.254. If any resolved address is private, refuse it.
options: Check that the page title is not an attack
Look up the name and check every address it resolves to with isPrivateHostname
Retry the check a second time

questions.q: A public page you fetch answers with a redirect to http://169.254.169.254/. How do you close that hole?
questions.explain: An automatic redirect sends your server to the private address without any check. With redirect: "manual" you see each target and run isSafeUrl and the DNS check on it.
options: Fetch with redirect: "manual" and check every redirect target the same way
Only fetch URLs that end in .html
Add the page to the CORS allow-list

questions.q: What is the real defence against SQL injection?
questions.explain: With parameters like $1 and $2, the database treats 1 or true as a value and refuses it for an integer column. Detectors and block-lists miss attacks and flag innocent text.
options: Parameterized queries: the input is sent to the database as a value, never pasted into the SQL text
Checking inputs with a regular expression block-list

questions.q: How should you use detectThreats?
questions.explain: It is a heuristic: it flagged "Please select a date and update the notes" and missed 1 or true. "No threats found" never means "safe".
options: Block every request it flags, and allow every request it does not flag
Log and alert on what it finds, to spot someone probing your API; never rely on it as the defence
Use it instead of schema validation

questions.q: A task title contains <script>. What stops it from running on your pages?
questions.explain: Encode text for the place it goes, so < becomes < and shows as text. CSP then blocks injected scripts even if encoding is missed somewhere.
options: Rejecting every title with a < in it
Encoding output for HTML (like escapeHtml) plus a strict CSP as a second layer
A CSRF token on the form

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: max: 2 allows two requests per window. remaining counts down to 0 and stays there; the third request is refused.

questions.q: An attacker sends a fake X-Forwarded-For. What does this print?
questions.explain: Without trustProxy, the header is ignored and the real connection address is used. That is what makes the fake header useless.

questions.q: Your own proxy at 10.0.0.1 forwards the request. What does this print?
questions.explain: With one trusted proxy, the address your proxy added (the last one) is used. 6.6.6.6 was written by the client before it and is ignored.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Only the exact origin passes. A longer name that starts with yours is a different host, and http is a different scheme, so both are refused.

questions.q: A developer forgot the anchors in a RegExp origin. What does this print?
questions.explain: Without ^ and $, the pattern only has to appear somewhere in the origin, so the evil host matches. The anchored version refuses it.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: createSecureCookie turns on the three attributes that matter: Secure, HttpOnly and SameSite=Lax.

questions.q: An attacker picks their own theme name. What does this print?
questions.explain: The value is percent-encoded, so ; and = become harmless text and cannot add a Domain attribute.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A DELETE changes data, so it needs the token in the header. With Ada's token it passes. HEAD is a safe method, like GET, so it passes without one.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A 6-character secret is far too weak to sign tokens, so the package refuses to start. It needs at least 32 characters of random data from the environment.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Each check returns an error message, or undefined when all is well. 20000 bytes is over the 16384 limit.
options:
Content-Length 512 is fine
Content-Length 20000 exceeds maximum 16384 bytes

questions.q: BODY_LIMIT is not set in the environment, so the code reads undefined. What does this print?
questions.explain: Number(undefined) is NaN, and every comparison with NaN is false. So a naive size > limit check lets a 5 GB body through. That is why createBodySizeChecker refuses a NaN limit.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: 0x7f000001 is 127.0.0.1 written in hex, 192.168.1.1 is a private address, and only http and https are allowed, so ftp is blocked too.

questions.q: A name resolves to two addresses. What does this print?
questions.explain: 10.0.0.8 is private. If any address is private, refuse the URL; checking only the first one would let this attacker through.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The heuristic flags an innocent sentence because it contains "drop", and misses 1 or true, which is a real attack. That is why detectors are for logging, not for protection.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Every <, > and & is encoded, so the browser shows the text instead of making it a tag. & must be encoded too, or text like < would turn back into a tag.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The strict defaults are X-Frame-Options: DENY (no framing at all) and X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff (no guessing file types).

questions.q: Write allowOrigin(origin, allowed) by hand. Return the origin when it is exactly one of the strings in allowed, otherwise return undefined. Do not use startsWith or includes on the string.
questions.explain: Compare with === against each entry (or allowed.includes(origin) on the array). origin.startsWith("https://app.example.com") would let https://app.example.com.evil.example through.

questions.q: Write isPrivateIPv4(address) for an SSRF check. Return true for 10.x.x.x, 127.x.x.x, 169.254.x.x, 192.168.x.x and 172.16.x.x to 172.31.x.x; otherwise false. Split the address on "." and compare numbers.
questions.explain: Look at the first two numbers. 172.16 to 172.31 is a range, so compare the second number as a number, not as text. In a real app use isPrivateHostname, which also knows IPv6 and odd spellings like 0x7f000001.

questions.q: A host name can resolve to several addresses. Finish checkAddresses(addresses): return "blocked" when the list is empty or when any address is private (use the given isPrivate), otherwise return "ok: " followed by the addresses joined with ", ".
questions.explain: Use some, not a check on the first address: the attacker mixes one public and one private address. An empty list means the name did not resolve, so refuse it too.

questions.q: Finish isFetchableUrl(text): return true only when the text parses with new URL, the protocol is "http:" or "https:", and the URL has no username or password. Return false when new URL throws.
questions.explain: Parse with new URL instead of looking at the text, and allow only the schemes you need. This is only the first step: the host must still be checked against private addresses.
questions.expected:
true https://example.com/a
false file:///etc/passwd
false http://user:pass@example.com/
false not a url
true http://example.com:8080/

questions.q: Build a tiny rate limiter. createLimiter(max) returns a function check(ip) that counts calls per IP in a Map and returns true while the count is at most max, and false after that.
questions.explain: Each IP has its own counter, so a new address starts at 1. A real limiter also resets the count when the time window ends; that is what windowMs does in createRateLimiter.

questions.q: Write escapeHtml(text) by hand. Replace & with &, < with <, > with > and " with ". Replace & first.
questions.explain: If you replaced < first, the next step would turn its & into & and break it. In a real app use escapeHtml from the package, and add a strict CSP.

questions.q: Finish needsCsrfToken(method): return false for the safe methods GET, HEAD and OPTIONS, and true for every other method. Accept lower-case method names too.
questions.explain: Every method that can change data needs the token. Safe methods pass without one, which is why a GET handler must never change data.
questions.expected: false true false true false true

questions.q: Finish readBodyLimit(text), which reads a limit from an environment variable. Return the number when it is finite and above 0. Otherwise throw an Error with the message BODY_LIMIT must be a positive number.
questions.explain: Number(undefined) and Number("abc") are NaN, and NaN makes every size comparison false. Refusing to start is safer than running with no limit.
questions.expected:
16384
BODY_LIMIT must be a positive number
BODY_LIMIT must be a positive number
BODY_LIMIT must be a positive number

questions.q: Finish secureCookie(name, value). Encode the value with encodeURIComponent and add the attributes Secure, HttpOnly and SameSite=Lax, separated by "; ".
questions.explain: Encoding the value stops an attacker from adding their own Domain or other attributes with ;. In the Task API, use createSecureCookie, which does the same.
questions.expected:
sid=f3a9c1; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax
theme=x%3B%20Domain%3Devil.example; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax
